editorial_thesis: The practical shift today is control-plane maturity: measure which agent actually works, isolate where it runs, and make every external integration explicitly admissible and observable.

topic_groups.title: Agent Portfolio Controls
topic_groups.selection_rationale: Yesterday’s GitHub releases turn agent rollout from a single adoption number into review depth, per-agent activity, and directional spend/output evidence—a fresh operational lane after recent runtime coverage.

sources.title: Copilot code review effort levels are generally available
sources.why_selected: GA effort levels make review depth a deliberate policy choice rather than an invisible model setting.
sources.usefulness: Map Lite and Balanced review to change risk in a client or Buildn repository.
sources.what: GitHub Copilot code review now offers GA Lite and Balanced effort levels, configurable per review or as organization defaults.
sources.matters: Routine documentation edits and cross-service or security-sensitive changes should not consume the same review budget.
sources.use: Set a default for routine changes; require Balanced on sensitive paths, migrations, and externally exposed code.
sources.caveat: Review effort is not an acceptance test. Preserve CI, human ownership, and security review for high-consequence changes.
sources.action: Write a one-page PR risk rubric that assigns Lite, Balanced, or human-only review.

sources.title: Copilot usage metrics API adds agent app activity
sources.why_selected: It separates recognized third-party agent activity by stable agent identifier in 1- and 28-day reports.
sources.usefulness: It supplies a practical schema for evaluating a mixed agent fleet rather than relying on anecdotes.
sources.what: The Copilot usage metrics API adds optional totals_by_3rd_party_agent entries, including agent_id, job starts, and aggregate session counts.
sources.matters: A shared “agent usage” bucket hides whether a new harness is complementing or displacing the one it was meant to improve.
sources.use: If a client uses GitHub enterprise controls, join reports on agent_id and compare adoption, cost, cycle time, and accepted output by agent.
sources.caveat: Unrecognized agents are omitted; job starts are not the same metric as top-level prompts, and activity is not outcome quality.
sources.action: Add agent_id, accepted PRs, rework rate, and human-review time to a 28-day experiment sheet.

sources.title: Copilot impact dashboard adds a return on investment section
sources.why_selected: It puts actual AI-credit-derived cost beside pull-request output for passive and agent-first adoption cohorts.
sources.usefulness: Use the framing to start a better client conversation about enablement without treating PR volume as ROI.
sources.what: GitHub’s impact dashboard adds a potential ROI view with cost per developer, payroll percentage, and pull requests per month across adoption cohorts.
sources.matters: The release makes the cost/output trade-off visible, while also showing why volume alone must not become the success metric.
sources.use: Pair dashboard data with defect escapes, reviewer burden, and delivery lead time before choosing an agent rollout path.
sources.caveat: GitHub labels the figures directional: salary is modeled, costs are estimates, and pull-request volume does not prove value or quality.
sources.action: Use the dashboard only as one panel in a scorecard with quality and cycle-time guardrails.

topic_groups.title: Bounded Agent Execution
topic_groups.selection_rationale: New browser and microVM options are concrete enough to test now, while avoiding a repeat of this week’s runtime/observability lens: the focus here is where untrusted work is allowed to execute.

sources.title: Introducing Kitesurf, an agent-first browser on Browser Run
sources.why_selected: It offers a stateless browser designed for agent workloads with an opt-in compatibility path through existing Browser Run endpoints.
sources.usefulness: It is a viable benchmark candidate for bursty screenshot and extraction jobs.
sources.what: Cloudflare’s Kitesurf is a beta stateless browser on Workers; Cloudflare reports 3–7× lower CPU and memory for common agent screenshots and HTML extraction.
sources.matters: Browser sessions are expensive and high-risk. Stateless, elastic execution can reduce capacity pressure when tasks are narrow and repeatable.
sources.use: Benchmark one research or QA job against the existing browser path, keeping credentials, uploads, and destructive interactions out of the trial.
sources.caveat: Vendor performance figures need workload-specific validation; beta status and browser compatibility differences can surface at the edges.
sources.action: Run a 20-job screenshot/extraction benchmark with latency, error, and fidelity checks.

sources.title: Vercel AI Gateway and Vercel Sandbox now available on Hermes Agent
sources.why_selected: The integration joins multi-model routing with a configurable microVM command backend in the agent workflow used for this ingest.
sources.usefulness: It gives a direct path to trial cloud-isolated commands without rebuilding the orchestration layer.
sources.what: Hermes Agent can use Vercel AI Gateway and switch terminal commands to Vercel Sandbox microVMs, with a workspace rooted in the sandbox.
sources.matters: Model access and command execution are separate boundaries; treating the latter as a backend makes containment an explicit operating choice.
sources.use: Prototype a client automation with read-only inputs and an isolated workspace, then promote only reviewed artifacts to the real repository.
sources.caveat: A sandbox limits execution blast radius but does not remove the need for secret scoping, egress policy, artifact review, or cost controls.
sources.action: Run one non-production task in a sandbox and document filesystem, network, credential, and promotion boundaries.

sources.title: Give every agent in Herdr its own Vercel Sandbox
sources.why_selected: It shows a practical multi-agent pattern: local orchestration with separate sandboxes, reviewed uploads, conflict checks, and human-confirmed deletion.
sources.usefulness: Borrow the boundary design even if neither product becomes the production platform.
sources.what: Herdr can assign terminal agents their own Vercel Sandboxes while retaining local orchestration and review controls around files and deletion.
sources.matters: Concurrency is safer when agents do not share mutable workspace state by default and transfers have named checkpoints.
sources.use: For parallel client work, give each agent a disposable branch/workspace and merge only reviewable patches with provenance.
sources.caveat: Isolation does not solve conflicting requirements or validate output. Human acceptance criteria still need to be explicit.
sources.action: Adopt per-task worktrees today; add stronger runtime isolation only after the workflow proves valuable.

topic_groups.title: Integration Trust Boundaries
topic_groups.selection_rationale: This lane fills a gap between agent capability and real deployment: current releases expose the three seams that fail first—tool admission, application permissions, and security-event evidence.

sources.title: MCP allowlists in enterprise managed settings
sources.why_selected: GitHub now provides centrally managed, fail-closed MCP allow/deny policies across Copilot app, CLI, and VS Code.
sources.usefulness: It is an immediately usable reference for a client MCP admission policy.
sources.what: Enterprise settings can allow or deny MCP servers by canonicalized remote URL, exact local command/arguments, or name; malformed or unverifiable configurations are blocked.
sources.matters: Tool discovery turns an integration into effective agent authority. An allowlist makes that authority reviewable before it reaches developer machines.
sources.use: Maintain a small approved-server inventory; match remote URLs or exact commands, not friendly server names, and specify an owner and renewal date.
sources.caveat: This is GitHub-specific enforcement. Names are explicitly not a security control, and policy coverage is limited to supported clients.
sources.action: Inventory every MCP server in use and classify it approved, experimental, blocked, or unknown.

sources.title: Enterprises can now install third-party GitHub Apps
sources.why_selected: It opens an enterprise-level installation path while preserving an important restriction for the most powerful organization-installation permissions.
sources.usefulness: It creates a clearer delivery route for Buildn integrations that need enterprise-management scope.
sources.what: GitHub enterprise owners can install external public GitHub Apps; apps with enterprise organization-installation permissions cannot be installed across enterprise boundaries.
sources.matters: Enterprise-level distribution is useful, but the permission model must be designed for the blast radius rather than for the easiest onboarding flow.
sources.use: For any client app, request the smallest permission set, document the installation scope, and avoid cross-enterprise plans if restricted permissions are required.
sources.caveat: Installing at enterprise scope does not grant organization or repository access by itself; every follow-on permission still needs explicit review.
sources.action: Create a permission table for the next GitHub App: user, org, repository, enterprise, data read, data write, and exit plan.

sources.title: Audit Log Drains now support Datadog, Splunk, and Panther
sources.why_selected: It adds direct audit-event destinations and a migration away from the prior custom SIEM streaming path.
sources.usefulness: It closes the evidence loop for hosted client delivery where deployment and configuration actions need independent visibility.
sources.what: Vercel Audit Log Drains now stream team activity events plus audit metadata to Datadog, Splunk, or Panther, alongside HTTPS and S3 destinations.
sources.matters: A permission boundary cannot be reviewed after an incident if deployment, access, and configuration actions remain trapped in a vendor console.
sources.use: For Enterprise clients, send audit logs to the existing detection platform and verify retention, alert ownership, and the migration from Custom SIEM Log Streaming.
sources.caveat: The feature is Enterprise-only; log forwarding is not monitoring until high-signal rules, retention, and response ownership are configured.
sources.action: Choose three auditable events—access change, production deploy, secret change—and prove they arrive in the team’s response system.
